en: Your father blustered, saying he would take her.)
“Gather the khojas and mullahs,” he said.
“Have prayers recited over this fiery woman;
Perform the marriage today!” he said.
When your father Manas sought to force her,
Insisting he would marry her,
The fine white dress with golden flowers
The maiden Saikal refused to wear.
Your father, the wolf-like sultan,
The maiden Saikal refused to marry.
“Peerless, wolf-like lord, hear my words.
I will not wear this dress of yours,
I will not marry you in this world.
What we see today is gone tomorrow;
Such is this filthy world.
I have no desire for this world.
Bloodthirsty lord, let me obey you thus:
As your bride in the life to come,
When Judgment dawns tomorrow,
I myself shall go
To join with you.
Let me be your bride for Judgment,
And you my husband in the other world.
At your death, for forty days,
I myself shall come, my king,
And stand in attendance at your honors.
The reason I myself
Will not be yours in this world is this:
The wife you have married
Is complete on every side,
A lion among women,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of Allah,
A dusky beauty,
The radiant one among Muslims,
The most capable of humankind,
The finest among women,
The purest bearer of a wife's name.
The wife you have married
Is queen of the broad-skirted women.
She is a true saint.
The wife you have married,
Kanykei, has a seal upon her tongue,
And a wart upon her lip.
Anyone she curses comes to no good;
Anyone her tongue strikes cannot remain unharmed.
I shall not settle along broad Talas.
With that sultan among women, Kanykei,
I shall not become a blustering rival wife.
Anyone this woman's tongue strikes comes to no good;
Anyone she fixes with her gaze remains unharmed no longer.
Coveting this faithless world,
I shall find no good in it.
A husband is dear in this world,
But blustering and contending over you,
I shall not bring shame upon myself.
I shall not do as you say,
I shall not marry you in this world.
If your wife's words strike me,
Like a horse-tethering post,
I shall depart utterly bare.
Without beholding God's face,
I shall depart an unbeliever.
I have known your wife before,
That queen among women,
That fierce woman with a prophet's nature.
With what face could I, poor soul,
Go about as her rival wife?
Here is the Kyrgyz land with its sovereign.
If you trample and humiliate me,
Here I am, if you would cut off my head!
Here is my blood, if you would spill it;
Here is my life, if you would take it.
Here are the people and warriors gathered round;
Here I am, if you would humiliate me!
Wolf-like hero, hear my words.
I shall not settle along these hills.
To your wife, Sultan Kanykei,
I shall not become a clamorous rival wife!”
When Khan Saikal, daughter of Khan Karacha,
Bowed her neck to the ground
And lay there refusing,
Bakai came to intervene,
But she remained unmoved in her refusal.
When the fierce woman would not obey,
A gray two-year colt born of a kulan
Was dedicated and slaughtered as a moon-hoofed sacrifice.
Aikojo in his patterned robe,
With Aikojo at their head,
Six khojas were summoned.
Making the promise firm,
Swearing an oath unto death,
His marriage for the life to come,
Your father, blessed by Khizir,
Had the khojas solemnize.
Then Saikal rejoiced:
“My king, it is now clear
That your world is complete.
The youngest of six lions,
You have shown yourself a hero.
Those who come upon your right,
Today you have shown you mow them down.
These Muslims gathered here—
Today you have shown you are their fortress.
Here is your sustenance when you enter battle.
Not knowing, I fought you fiercely with my spear.
Hero, do not make me suffer for my fault.”
Speaking these words then,
Karacha's Saikal
Said, “This shall be your travel ration,”
And gave him grain the size of a fist.
“My king, at Kokotoi's memorial feast,
Before the great assembly,
When Koshoi gave his blessing,
Unbelievers and Muslims
Gave their blessings together—
My father Karacha
Heard this and told me so.
Hero, to you yourself
A child conceived through that blessing
Is destined to come.
For the hope within your heart,
Let me assign a yearling foal
To your child still in the womb, hero.
Let me tell you about the foal.
There, where the corners loomed in haze,
Where the crags were dim and misty,
On this side of Barbar,
Beside the Lop River,
In the season of early thaw,
In the marshes of Ken-Ozon,
Seventy mares were foaling.
While they lay in Ken-Ozon,
When dawn broke clear,
When light touched the earth,
Amid a swirling, blustering squall,
While the wind was blowing,
I rode to a certain place.
A whirlwind was dancing there.
But it was no whirlwind:
A foal was frolicking there.
No mother said, ‘I bore it,’
No father said, ‘I begot it.’
It appeared from the unseen world,
A creature beloved by God,
Found thus in the open country.
Its mother was a hidden spirit of the wilds;
From that day to this,
Its origins remain unknown.
Ride it six months: it will not tire.
Until sixty years of maturity,
Its grinding teeth will not be worn with age.
Ride it to Zhet-Kait: it will not tire.
Until seventy years of maturity,
He does not grow old by raising his tongue,
High-backed, yet low in stature,
It will not falter when ridden into the hills.
My noble lord, mark this:
It is far above Ak-kula,
Far surpasses Chalkuiruk,
Stands a head above Maaniker.
Konurbai's Algara
Used to belong to our herd;
It is far above Alkara,
Higher still than Kulansur,
And far above Telkuron.
Ride it hard with your heels: it will not grow saddle-sore.
The wind cannot match its trot;
No beast can match its walk.
When grown, it will be the horse Buurul.
If you live, you shall see.
Whoever asks for it will become a stranger.”
To your father, wolf-like Manas,
She gave Taibuurul as a gift.
I received him as a yearling.
When he came to Taragai,
He was a worn-out roan foal.
When I opened his mouth and looked,
He had an extra tooth.
I had his extra tooth knocked out.
Lest he freeze to death,
Lest his end come in that way,
I had a fine horse-cover laid over him.
I had sixty foals killed at once,
And let him suck a little from their mothers.
With mortal difficulty I had him reared thus.
I had owl feathers fastened to his head,
Lest someone's evil eye strike him,
And had him reared where no one could see him.
When he reached two years,
I trained his neck to turn like a deer's.
If a ditch a target's distance wide appeared,
He galloped on without hesitation.
Once he recognized the steed's excellence,
Offering gold and precious cloth by the pood,
The lord of Bukhara asked for him.
I did not give him to anyone who asked.
Far from giving him away,
I let no one mount the steed without ablutions.
When you ride Buurul, my foal,
He is your Buraq left by your father Manas.
When you mount your Buurul
And set out this way,
Do not blunt your steel.
Your father's Aktulpar—
Do not lose Aktulpar.
Your grandfather Temirkan
Was a malicious khan,
A man miserly with livestock.
Because of what happened before,
On account of Aktulpar,
Oiumkan, whom Ormombek married,
Was a sister of mine too.
He earned a name by raising a thoroughbred;
On account of Aktulpar,
That son-in-law left and became a stranger.
Zhamgyrchy of the Eshteks
Was a son-in-law too.
On account of Aktulpar,
This son-in-law left and became a stranger.
Hero Shygai of the Zhediger
Was a son-in-law too.
On account of Aktulpar,
That son-in-law left and became a stranger.
He who summered in Eki-Kemin,
Tethered a pair of black horses,
Honed his sharp tongue,
Spoke eloquently before the khan,
Sowed his rice as an autumn crop,
Fed the millet from his rice fields
To his tethered racer,
Made a dark cave his home,
Made the dense forest his wealth,
Reared a harrier into a hunting bird,
Gathered mixed peoples into a nation,
Reared an unruly bird into a hunting bird,
Made wanderers into a people,
Laced together the yurt's lattice,
Brought an obstinate people into order—
Hero Urbu, son of Khan Eibit.
He was a son-in-law too.
Because of what happened before,
On account of Aktulpar,
He cut a twig to sever ties, finding no good there;
The son-in-law Urbu became a stranger.
My golden crown, Muzburchak,
Who dwelt in Zhelpinish,
To whom seven unseen spirits gave a coat,
To whom seven saints lent their hands,
Who spent nights at sacred tombs,
Whom wary enemies did not approach—
My golden crown, Muzburchak,
Was a son-in-law too.
On account of Aktulpar,
That son-in-law left and became an enemy.
